subject: The 1971 D.B. Cooper hijacking — the only unsolved skyjacking in U.S. history
central_question: How did a calm man in a business suit hijack a passenger jet, collect $200,000, parachute into a freezing night over the Pacific Northwest, and vanish so completely that, more than fifty years later, the FBI still cannot say who he was?
viewer_promise: By the end, the viewer understands the hijacking minute by minute, what the one recovered clue does and doesn't prove, every serious suspect theory weighed without accusing anyone, and why the FBI finally suspended the case it never solved.
surprise: Most people assume a crime broadcast on national news, with a money trail and a 45-year manhunt, must eventually be solved. In fact no one was ever charged, the man was never identified, most of the cash was never found, and in 2016 the FBI suspended the case, leaving the most famous unsolved hijacking in history exactly where it began.
stakes: The identity and fate of a man who pulled off a seemingly perfect crime, $200,000 that mostly vanished with him, a single decaying bundle of bills as the only physical trail, and a legend that has outlived nearly everyone who chased it.
target_audience: English-speaking general audience skewing men 40+ who love true-crime, heists, aviation, Cold-War-era Americana, and unsolved mysteries
demand_evidence: D.B. Cooper is one of the most recognized unsolved mysteries in America; heist-plus-disappearance content is a top evergreen genre with durable search interest.
A genuine open case drives rewatch, theory comments, and strong like/engagement signals.
competition: Much existing coverage pushes a single pet suspect or drowns in trivia; few neutrally walk the full minute-by-minute crime, the one hard clue, every theory weighed fairly, and the legal reason the FBI suspended it.
differentiation: A clean, cinematic unsolved mystery built for a 40+ male audience: a tense minute-by-minute reconstruction, the physics of the jump, the boy and the buried money, theories weighed without accusing anyone, and the haunting 'suspended, not solved' ending. Primary-source (FBI) based, neutral, advertiser-safe, symbolic visuals with no real-person likeness.
research_feasibility: High: the FBI maintains a public D.B. Cooper (NORJAK) case page and a 2016 suspension press release; strong secondary coverage (HISTORY, Smithsonian, Seattle Times, HistoryLink) corroborates.
visual_feasibility: High: symbolic reconstruction of a 1971 jet cabin, a passed note, a briefcase, a parachute, an open aft airstair into a stormy night, a riverbank money find, a corkboard of theories. No real-person likeness.
risk_notes: UNSOLVED case. The FBI never charged, identified, or confirmed any suspect. NEVER assert or imply any named person 'was D.B. Cooper' or committed the crime. Use 'named as / proposed as / investigated as a suspect', attributed to whoever proposed them.
Most named suspects are deceased; the status of some is unverified. Never accuse a living person; do not state a living/deceased status that is not confirmed.

Several details vary across sources (exact jump time and location, the 'D.B.' name-error mechanism, the tipping anecdote). Phrase cautiously and attribute. The FBI gives no passenger number and only a broad jump corridor.
Crew and victims (flight attendants, pilots) are named only as on the record, neutrally. No real-person likeness in AI visuals (invariant 11).
Generated visuals are symbolic reconstruction, never presented as authentic 1971 footage.
kill_conditions: Cannot source the hijacking mechanics, the ransom/parachute facts, the 1980 money find, and the unsolved/suspended status to the FBI plus independent reporting.
Cannot present the suspect theories without risking accusation of a living person.
